newsitem.title: CHINA: Just 20 percent of China families have one child.
newsitem.headline: Just 20 percent of China families have one child.

text.p: Just one-fifth of Chinese families have a single child despite Beijing's official family planning policy promoting one child per couple, officials said on Wednesday.
Of China's 320 million families, just 20.72 percent have only one child, an official with the China Family Planning Commission quoted a recent government survey as showing.

The official said the figure was not unexpected but international population workers voiced surprise, saying China's official policy of limiting most couples to one child should have resulted in many more single child families.
"It seems low," said Junko Sazaki, deputy representative of the United Nations Population Fund in China.
The Chinese official did not say what age group the survey covered and gave no breakdown of rural and urban families.

China, the world's most populous nation with 1.2 billion people, launched its strict one-child policy in the late 1970s amid fears that rapidly growing numbers of people would soon outstrip resources and hamper economic growth.
The policy was an about-face from the ideas of Chairman Mao Zedong, who believed that a large population would make China powerful.

China has punished couples who have more than one child with fines and losses of education privileges, but nearly two decades of market-style economic reform have enabled many families to afford to ignore the policy.
"It is not a matter of the number, it's a matter of the number of children they can be responsible for," Sazaki said.
The reforms have also allowed people to work and travel more freely, thus eroding the state's control over their lives and making enforcement of the one-child rule more difficult.
"People are very smart in getting around any restrictions imposed by the government," Sazaki said.

Beijing has come under fire from Western human rights groups that say the one-child policy has led to forced abortions and the killing of baby girls by parents hoping for a son to carry on the family line.
The policy also has many loopholes, such as allowing rural and ethnic minority couples to have more than one child.
"There are some exceptions, but the family planning policy has never changed," the Chinese official said. "It is hard to tell what the future of family planning is, but we are not changing it now."
China had 1.224 billion people at the end of 1996, up 12.68 million from the year before and with a natural population growth of 10.42 per 1,000, latest official figures show.
China's communist rulers have said controlling the population to within 1.3 billion people at the end of the century is essential to help to erase poverty and protect the environment.
